explain.say: Look at a motorcycle engine, a laptop cooler or an electric motor: they all bristle with thin metal blades. Why? Convection loss is h times A times delta T. Air is a poor carrier of heat, so h stays small. The easy fix is a bigger area. Follow the chain of reasons on the board.

explain.say: But a fin only helps if heat can travel along it. The base is hot; the tip is cooler, because heat leaks out of the sides as it goes. See the graph: an aluminium fin, 2 millimetres thick and 30 long, with an 80 degree base in 20 degree air, cools only to about 74 degrees at the tip.

explain.say: A steel fin, with a quarter of the conductivity, drops to about 60 degrees at the tip. See the lower curve? A cooler fin sheds less heat. Fin efficiency compares the real heat flow with a fin that is at base temperature everywhere. For aluminium it is 93 percent, for steel 78. So which metal makes the better heat sink?

explain.say: Aluminium: good conductivity, light and cheap. Copper is even better, but heavy. Now effectiveness: one 50 millimetre wide aluminium fin sheds about 8.4 watts. The bare patch of base it stands on would shed only 0.3 watts. So the fin is about 28 times better than no fin.

explain.say: Brilliant. Real link: fins work best in air, where h is low, and are rarely worth it in boiling water, where h is already huge. Exam tip: making a fin very long adds little, because the far end is nearly at air temperature. Challenge: why are fins thin and close, but not touching?

faq.q: Why do heat sinks have fins?
faq.a: Convection heat loss grows with surface area, and air has a low heat transfer coefficient. Fins add a lot of extra area in a small space, so much more heat can escape.

faq.q: Why is the fin tip cooler than the base?
faq.a: Heat leaks out of the sides as it conducts along the fin, so less and less heat reaches the far end and its temperature falls towards the air temperature.
asks: why are heat sinks made of aluminium

faq.a: The actual heat a fin sheds divided by the heat it would shed if the whole fin were at the base temperature. For a straight fin with an insulated tip it is tanh of m L over m L.
The heat a fin sheds divided by the heat the bare base area would shed without it. Fins are only worth adding if effectiveness is well above 1, usually above about 2.

faq.q: When are fins not worth using?
faq.a: When h is already very high, as in boiling or fast water flow, because the bare surface already sheds heat well and the fin barely helps.

facts: For a straight fin with an insulated tip, efficiency = tanh(mL)/(mL), where m = √(hP/kA).
Aluminium is the most common heat-sink metal: it conducts well and is light.

quiz.say: A heat sink has a fin efficiency of 0.9. If a fin at base temperature everywhere would shed 10 watts, how much does it really shed?
quiz.show: Fin efficiency 0.9; ideal fin (all at base temperature) sheds 10 W. Actual heat?

wrong.1: That divides by the efficiency; a real fin sheds less than the ideal, not more.
wrong.2: That ignores the temperature drop along the fin.
